content: Harvest mites, also known as red bugs, trombiculid mites, scrub-itch mites, berry bugs, or chiggers in their larval stage, are small arachnids belonging to the family Trombiculidae. These mites are typically found in forests and grasslands. During their larval stage, they attach to various animals, including humans, and feed on skin cells, often causing intense itching. The larvae are microscopic, measuring about 0.4 mm in size, and exhibit a chrome-orange coloration. In North America, the most common species of harvest mite is Trombicula alfreddugesi, while in the United Kingdom, Trombicula autumnalis is more prevalent. The larval mites are immature forms that exist between the egg and nymph stages and have not yet developed into adult mites. These larvae are often found in berry patches, tall grass, weeds, woodland edges, pine straw, leaves, and tree bark, as well as in habitats frequented by their hosts, such as rodents. Harvest mite larvae feed on the skin cells of animals, including humans, but do not consume blood. These six-legged parasitic larvae feed on a wide range of hosts, including humans, rabbits, toads, box turtles, quail, and even some insects. Upon attaching to their host, the larvae inject digestive enzymes into the skin, which break down skin cells. They do not bite in the traditional sense but instead create a hole in the skin and consume liquefied tissue, leading to significant irritation and swelling. This process results in severe itching, accompanied by red, pimple-like bumps (papules), hives, or skin rashes, particularly in sun-exposed areas. Itching typically begins after the larvae detach from the skin. Chiggers do not spread from one host to another. After feeding, the larvae drop to the ground, transition into nymphs, and eventually mature into eight-legged adults, which are harmless to humans. In their post-larval stages, they are non-parasitic and feed on plant materials. Female mites lay 3–8 eggs in plant litter, often on leaves or under plant roots, and die by autumn. Chiggers are found in many parts of the world. In Europe and North America, they are more common in hot and humid regions. In temperate areas, they are typically present only during the summer months. For example, in French, they are referred to as aoûtat, meaning August flies. In the United States, chiggers are most prevalent in the Southeast, South, and Midwest, while they are rare or absent in far northern regions, high mountains, and deserts. Although harvest mites in North America generally do not transmit diseases, they are considered dangerous pests in East Asia and the South Pacific. In these regions, they often carry Rickettsia tsutsugamushi (also known as Orientia tsutsugamushi), the causative agent of scrub typhus, also referred to as Japanese river disease or tsutsugamushi disease. The mites acquire the infection from their rodent hosts and pass it on to their offspring through reproduction. Symptoms of scrub typhus in humans include fever, headache, muscle pain, cough, and gastrointestinal issues. In North America, heavy infestations of chiggers can cause severe illness in children, with symptoms such as fatigue, fever, general malaise, and hallucinations involving a sensation of floating outside the body. Contrary to popular belief, chigger larvae do not burrow deep into the skin or live there. Instead, they pierce the skin and inject enzymes that digest cellular contents, which are then consumed by the larvae. Another myth is that applying rubbing alcohol kills chiggers or alleviates symptoms. This method only causes significant burning pain and discomfort. The most effective way to remove chiggers is by taking a hot shower and washing the affected areas with mildly hot water and soap as soon as possible after exposure. Special attention should be given to areas such as the ankles, feet, behind the knees, under the arms, and the chest. An Epsom salt bath may help relieve itching. Wading in saltwater near the seashore can also remove mites from the skin and clothing while alleviating itching. Another method involves using scotch tape to remove the mites by sticking and pulling them off. However, once symptoms appear, it may be too late to prevent further irritation. Taking a hot bath after chigger bites may increase discomfort and itching. Scratching the skin aggressively should be avoided, as it can lead to increased irritation and potential secondary infections. Covering the itchy area with calamine lotion, petroleum jelly, or baby oil may help reduce discomfort but does not cure the bites. Applying clear nail polish to the bites is a popular remedy that may reduce itching and dry the sores if done early. However, the red dot in the center of the bite is often mistaken for the chigger itself, which is no longer present. Doctors may prescribe antihistamines or corticosteroid creams to alleviate symptoms in some cases. Preventive measures include wearing tight-weave, protective clothing, and long pants, applying insect repellent to the skin, and treating shoes and lower trousers with repellents. Staying on trails and avoiding tall grass or thick vegetation can also reduce exposure. Dusting sulfur on shoes, socks, and trouser legs is highly effective in repelling chiggers. People picking wild blueberries in the summer are particularly vulnerable to chigger bites and may benefit from applying deodorant soap to the skin and letting it dry without rinsing. Recognizing chigger habitats and avoiding them is another effective strategy. In North America, chiggers thrive in late summer in dry, tall grasses and unshaded vegetation. Insect repellents containing DEET, catnip oil extract (Nepetalactone), citronella, or eucalyptus oil extract are recommended. A study published in the Southeast Asian Journal of Tropical Medicine & Public Health in March 1993 found that DEET was more effective than citrus oil in repelling chiggers. Additionally, common household vinegar (5% acetic acid) has been reported as a treatment for chiggers, as noted in the Archives of Internal Medicine on March 12, 2001.
